body_markdown:
As of this summer, I am now the proud owner of a pickup truck. It’s unlocked a few things for me, from expanded project capacity to boosted confidence that I’ll be able to handle whatever’s ahead of me. Both of those are probably placebo effects, but I will never *not* own a pickup again in my life. They are simply too useful.


But in the months after the truck was delivered, I’ve begun to notice a creeping sentiment: What about owning one truck makes me *want a second truck* ? Perhaps more importantly, why does my desire for a second truck skew decidedly old-school and compact?

This[1986 Jeep Comanche XLS, currently available on Hagerty Marketplace](https://www.hagerty.com/marketplace/auction/1986-Jeep-Comanche/1dc450ed-a051-4119-9da7-185a78e866df) , is doing nothing to quell those feelings. In fact, it’s enflaming them to an alarming degree.


In the mid-1980s, AMC Chairman W. Paul Tippett Jr. told *Time* magazine that “People are finding trucks a reasonable and sophisticated alternative to cars.” He was right, and his company knew it needed to capitalize on the shifting trend.[The Comanche](https://www.hagerty.com/media/member-stories/this-jeep-comanche-has-always-climbed-mountains/) , which debuted in late summer of 1985 as a 1986 model, was the result. It was based heavily on the[XJ Jeep Cherokee](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/jeeps-xj-cherokee-makes-a-strong-case-for-the-practical-classic/) , which debuted in 1984.

Marketplace/J.Smith1985


Marketplace/J.Smith1985


Built from 1986–92, the Comanche has always felt like an odd duck, probably because of the badge on the hood. By this time period, Jeep had made a respectable—if not enviable—name for itself building wildly capable, simple machines that could take you where few other vehicles could. They galvanized the SUV space around the idea of adventure and exploration, and when your brand becomes so good at one thing, it can be hard to shake that preconceived notion. “Jeep,” to most consumers of the day, probably meant a four-wheel-drive SUV. Meeting a pickup with that badge may have been a surprise.


Marketplace/J.Smith1985


For what was likely a multitude of reasons, the Comanche never really took off. Other more established players in the compact truck segment—namely the[Ford Ranger](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/how-to-solve-a-midlife-crisis-with-the-car-you-already-have/) and the Chevrolet S10—had far more clout and outsold the Jeep by hefty multiples. By 1992, the Comanche had reached the end of the road.


Marketplace/J.Smith1985


This example looks remarkably well preserved. It’s a first-year rendition replete with part-time four-wheel drive, an Aisin five-speed manual transmission, and a 2.8-liter V-6 that, ironically, was the same six-pot used in the Chevy S-10. According to the listing, A Weber carburetor has been fitted in place of the original two-barrel Rochester unit.


Marketplace/J.Smith1985


Marketplace/J.Smith1985


The Olympic White paint job still looks quite solid, and those orange 4×4 graphics have exactly the right level of wear on them. These little fellas represent the epitome of the “it’s a truck, it’s a tool, I use it as such” mentality that the greatest salt-of-the-earth people you know still carry. This Comanche is the exact right level of weathered for my taste, and I can’t help but picture it parked next to my existing half-ton as a weekend errand mobile and all-around fun-box.


As of this writing, there are 12 days left in the sale. If you’ve been looking for the perfect pocket pickup to add to park beside your Nimitz-Class Ford F-350 or your Ram 3500, this might be the ticket.
